value.scenario: You need ordered operations (range queries, floor/ceil) AND guaranteed fast lookup on data that keeps changing.

approaches.label: A plain (unbalanced) BST
approaches.rejectionFeedback: A plain BST supports ordered queries but can degrade to an O(n)-height chain on bad insert orders, losing the guaranteed fast lookup.

approaches.label: A hash map
approaches.rejectionFeedback: A dict maintains insertion order, not sorted-key order. Without another index, range/floor/ceiling queries require scanning keys.

reasons.text: A balanced BST keeps height O(log n), guaranteeing O(log n) search/insert/delete while its in-order structure answers range and floor/ceil queries.
A hash map answers range and floor/ceil queries efficiently.
A plain BST always has O(log n) height regardless of insertion order.

value.modelExplanation: A balanced BST (AVL/red-black) gives guaranteed O(log n) search/insert/delete AND ordered queries. A plain BST risks O(n) if unbalanced; a hash map is expected O(1) but supports no order/range queries.

value.scenario: You need to list all stored words matching a prefix for repeated autocomplete queries. Which structure provides a prefix index, and what is the cost including copied suggestion characters?

approaches.label: A hash set of words
approaches.rejectionFeedback: A hash set only answers exact membership; it cannot efficiently find all words sharing a prefix, which is exactly what autocomplete needs.

reasons.text: A trie supplies a prefix index: reach the prefix, visit S subtree nodes and copy K output characters in expected O(P+S+K).
A hash set finds all words with a given prefix in O(P) just like a trie.
The reason to pick a trie is that exact membership is faster than a hash set.

value.modelExplanation: A trie reaches the prefix in expected O(P) and walks S subtree nodes. Copying K output characters gives O(P+S+K) for full enumeration; a hash set must scan its stored words.

value: Find the node representing the prefix.
Repeated scans of all stored words repeat prefix comparisons.
A trie shares those comparisons on one path.
Walk the matching subtree and collect terminal paths.
Use a shared character buffer; copy it only for terminal output strings.
Reaching the prefix costs expected O(P), traversal O(S), and copied output O(K), for O(P+S+K).

value.scenario: You must search a character grid for MANY words at once, deciding whether to search each word separately or share work across them.

approaches.label: Build a trie of all words and run one trie-guided DFS
Run a separate single-word DFS for each word
approaches.rejectionFeedback: Searching each word independently re-explores the same grid paths once per word (O(m·n·3^L) each), wasting the work shared by common prefixes.

reasons.text: A trie shares comparisons among words along each grid path, pruning a path when no dictionary prefix can continue; different grid paths can still repeat a prefix.
The words share no prefixes, so a trie saves nothing over separate searches.
A trie-guided DFS is slower than repeating single-word DFS because the trie adds overhead.

value.modelExplanation: Build a trie of all the words and run one DFS (Word Search II): walk the grid guided by the trie so shared prefixes are explored once, instead of paying O(m·n·3^L) separately per word.

value.scenario: You need shortest distances between ALL pairs of vertices in a small, dense graph (V ≈ 200, edges ≈ V²).

approaches.label: Binary-heap Dijkstra from every vertex
approaches.rejectionFeedback: For dense input the binary-heap upper bound adds a logarithmic factor; Floyd–Warshall is a simple cubic all-pairs choice. Array-based dense Dijkstra is also cubic, so this comparison is specific to the heap variant.

reasons.text: Floyd–Warshall is O(V³) with tiny triple-loop code, and on a dense graph that beats the O(V³ log V) of Dijkstra-from-every-source while being far simpler.
Floyd–Warshall is asymptotically slower than Dijkstra-from-every-source on dense graphs.
Floyd–Warshall only computes paths from a single source.

value.modelExplanation: Floyd–Warshall: O(V³) with tiny code; on a dense graph, Dijkstra from every source is ~O(V³ log V). Floyd–Warshall avoids the log factor and is simpler for all-pairs on dense/small graphs.

value.scenario: Return the average value of the nodes on each level of a binary tree.

approaches.label: Tree BFS (level order with a queue)

reasons.text: Process the tree level by level: snapshot the queue length each iteration to isolate one level and average its values — O(n).
The task needs a running path sum down each root-to-leaf route.
Node values must be sorted before averaging.
Carry each node’s depth in DFS and update a sum/count bucket for that depth. This also computes level averages in O(n).

value.modelExplanation: BFS with a queue-size snapshot is direct; DFS carrying depth into sum/count buckets is also a valid O(n) solution.

value.scenario: Find the maximum root-to-leaf path sum. Tree BFS or Tree DFS?

reasons.text: A path problem needs to carry a running sum down each root-to-leaf route, which recursion (DFS) does naturally — O(n).
The work is defined per level, so a breadth-first queue is the fit.
You must keep a heap of partial sums to solve it.
Queue pairs (node, running total), update the maximum at leaves, and pass the extended total to children. This also visits each node once.

value.modelExplanation: DFS carries path totals with O(h) frames; BFS carrying (node,total) is also correct, using O(w) frontier storage. Both take O(n) time.

value: The task compares totals at leaves, not level totals.
A traversal must preserve the sum along each node’s root path.
DFS can pass the running sum as an argument; BFS can queue it alongside the node.
Use DFS for a natural O(h)-frame implementation or BFS with (node,total) pairs.
At each node add its value; at leaves compare with the best; otherwise propagate the total to children.
Both traversals take O(n); their frontier storage differs: O(h) for DFS and O(w) for BFS.
Siblings should appear in the same output group.
The starter removes one node per outer round and therefore creates one group per node.
At a round’s beginning the queue contains exactly the next whole level.
Save its size before adding children, then remove that many nodes.

range(len(q)) evaluates its length once, isolating the current level even while children are appended.

value.scenario: Find all root-to-leaf paths whose values sum to a target.

approaches.label: Tree BFS
approaches.rejectionFeedback: Level-order processing does not carry the current path and running sum needed to record qualifying routes.

reasons.text: Tree DFS carrying a shared path and running total, copying matching leaf paths and backtracking: O(n+K) time, O(h) auxiliary space, plus O(K) output values.
The task groups nodes by depth, so a queue-based level sweep fits.
The tree must be a BST and sorted for this to work.

value.modelExplanation: Tree DFS carrying a shared path and running total, copying matching leaf paths and backtracking: O(n+K) time, O(h) auxiliary space, plus O(K) output values.

value: Record complete root-to-leaf paths whose totals match.
Rebuilding ancestors repeatedly repeats work; copying saved paths still costs output size.
Maintain one current path and running total during DFS.
At a matching leaf save a copy, then undo the path append before returning.
append; add value; if matching leaf: record path[:]; recurse as needed; pop.
Traversal costs O(n) and copied output K costs O(K): O(n+K) time with O(h) working path/frames.

value.scenario: Return the values of the tree grouped by level. Tree DFS or Tree BFS?

reasons.text: Grouping by level is breadth-first work: a queue processes one full level at a time — O(n).
The task needs a running path sum, so recursion is natural.
Two heaps are needed to balance the levels.
Carry the depth in DFS and append each node to the bucket for that depth, visiting left before right to preserve per-level left-to-right order.

value.modelExplanation: BFS queue-size rounds group levels directly. DFS with depth buckets also works in O(n), visiting left before right for the usual level order.

value.scenario: Count the number of islands in a grid of land and water cells.

reasons.text: Treat land cells as nodes connected to adjacent land; launch a DFS from each unvisited land cell and count one component per launch — O(V+E).
Edges arrive incrementally, so a near-constant incremental union is required.
You need the shortest weighted path, so Dijkstra applies.
Create a set for each land cell, union side-adjacent land cells, then count distinct land roots. This also counts static islands.

value.modelExplanation: Flood-fill DFS/BFS is a direct O(V+E) static solution. Union-Find over land cells is also correct, with O(V+E*α(V)) amortized processing and extra DSU state.

value.scenario: The graph is FIXED and you need to count its connected components exactly once.

reasons.text: The graph does not change and you count once, so a single traversal launching a search per unvisited node is simplest — O(V+E).
When edges arrive incrementally or many connectivity queries are made, Union-Find's near-constant operations avoid re-traversing the whole graph.
You need shortest weighted paths, so a heap is required.
Start with V components, union every undirected edge and decrement the count on each successful merge. This is also valid for a one-time static count.

value.modelExplanation: A single DFS/BFS sweep is direct for static components. Union-Find also works: initialize V sets, union each edge and count surviving groups. Prefer DSU when connectivity updates or queries repeat.

value.scenario: Recognize: 'Find the minimum total travel time from a source to every city, given roads with positive times.' Which pattern? Choose the efficient standard default for unequal nonnegative edge weights.

approaches.label: Plain BFS
approaches.rejectionFeedback: BFS counts edges, not weighted cost; with unequal positive weights fewest-edges is not cheapest.

approaches.label: Bellman–Ford
approaches.rejectionFeedback: Bellman–Ford is also correct for nonnegative weights, but its O(V+V*E) bound is slower than the heap default requested here.

reasons.text: Weights are non-negative, so repeatedly settling the closest unvisited city and relaxing its roads via a min-heap is correct — O((V+E) log V).
All roads take the same time, so counting edges equals counting cost.
Some roads have negative time, so the closest-is-final rule breaks.

value.modelExplanation: Dijkstra's algorithm: a min-heap by distance settles the closest city and relaxes its edges; non-negative weights guarantee correctness — O((V+E) log V).

value: A query path may exist without a complete stored word ending there.
The dictionary needs a terminal marker separate from all character edges.
The unique end object cannot collide with a real character such as $.
After consuming every query character, require the end key in the final node.
Build character edges; mark node[end] for each inserted word; search the query path; return end in node.
Path existence proves only a prefix. The unique terminal key proves a complete word, including the empty word.
